difficultyReason: Classic correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers. Students must verify the stimulus commits the causal inference rather than a sampling or scope error.
stimulus: A study of urban neighborhoods found that areas with a higher density of coffee shops also had lower rates of violent crime. The city council should therefore encourage the opening of new coffee shops throughout the city, since coffee shops clearly reduce violent crime.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all neighborhoods based on a sample drawn only from urban areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two phenomena for evidence that one phenomenon causes the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without warrant that the city council has the authority to regulate business openings

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider whether the density of coffee shops varies by time of day

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that reducing violent crime might itself cause neighborhoods to attract more coffee shops

explanations.correct: The argument observes a correlation — coffee shop density and lower crime rates co-occur — and infers that the coffee shops cause the lower crime. That is a textbook correlation-causation error; the evidence supports association, not causation.
explanations.A: The study is explicitly of urban neighborhoods, and the conclusion targets city neighborhoods, so the scope is consistent. No unrepresentative sample flaw is committed here.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument takes co-occurrence as proof of a causal direction, which is unwarranted by the correlational data alone.
explanations.C: The city council's authority is not at issue in the argument; this concern is extraneous to the reasoning.
explanations.D: Time-of-day variation is a peripheral detail that would not undermine the core logical structure even if addressed.
explanations.E: This is a tempting trap — reversed causation is a real flaw — but the argument doesn't address direction at all; it simply infers causation from correlation. (E) correctly names reversed causation but mis-locates it as the primary error. The structural fault is treating correlation as causation in the first place.

difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap with a plausible 'right flaw, reversed' trap. Students must distinguish which direction the swap runs.
stimulus: To be admitted to the bar, a candidate must pass the bar examination. Marcus passed the bar examination last month. It follows that Marcus has been admitted to the bar.
questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for bar admission as though it were merely necessary for it

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to establish that passing the bar examination is a reliable indicator of legal competence

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition necessary for bar admission as though it were sufficient for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an individual from a general rule that applies only to groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without justification that the bar examination is the only requirement for practicing law

explanations.correct: Passing the bar exam is stated as a necessary condition for admission (you must pass to be admitted), but the argument concludes that because Marcus passed, he has been admitted. That treats the necessary condition as if it were sufficient — the classic necessary/sufficient swap.
explanations.A: This describes the opposite error: treating a sufficient condition as merely necessary. The bar exam is a necessary, not sufficient, condition, so this reverses the flaw.
explanations.B: Whether the exam measures competence is irrelevant to the logical structure of the argument about admission.
explanations.C: Correct. Passing is required for admission but does not by itself guarantee it; the argument assumes it does.
explanations.D: The rule applies to all individual candidates; no group-versus-individual confusion is present.
explanations.E: This is close to the correct flaw but frames it as an unstated assumption about law practice rather than identifying the logical error in the conditional reasoning.

difficultyReason: Ad hominem / circumstantial flaw with one trap that correctly names the flaw category but misapplies it, and one that describes a real but minor weakness.
stimulus: Dr. Pelham argues that the proposed pharmaceutical merger will harm consumer access to affordable medications. But Dr. Pelham is a paid consultant for one of the competitor firms that would benefit from blocking the merger. We should therefore disregard her analysis of the merger's effects.
questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes that the pharmaceutical merger would necessarily reduce competition in the market

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses a claim by questioning the motives of the person making it rather than addressing the substance of the claim

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether the competitor firm that employs Dr. Pelham also opposes the merger

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a conflict of interest with proof that the claim in question is false

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the merger's effects without consulting an independent economic analysis

explanations.correct: The argument attacks Dr. Pelham's financial interest rather than engaging with her analysis of the merger's effects. This is the circumstantial ad hominem flaw: impugning the person's motives as a basis for rejecting their argument.
explanations.A: The argument does not assume anything about the merger itself; it only dismisses Dr. Pelham's testimony. This flaw is absent from the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct. Regardless of Dr. Pelham's financial ties, those ties do not show her analysis is wrong. The argument should address the evidence she presents.
explanations.C: Whether her employer also opposes the merger is a peripheral factual detail irrelevant to the logical flaw in dismissing her testimony.
explanations.D: This is a tempting trap — it correctly identifies that the conflict of interest is misused — but it frames the error as a confusion rather than the structural ad hominem move. (B) more precisely names the reasoning error as described in LSAT flaw vocabulary.
explanations.E: Calling for an independent analysis describes a remedy, not the flaw in the existing reasoning.

difficultyReason: False dichotomy with a scope-shift trap. Students must see that the argument ignores intermediate options rather than making a statistical error.
stimulus: Our city's public schools are failing students academically. The school board must choose between completely overhauling the current curriculum and abandoning public education altogether in favor of a voucher-based private school system. Since a complete curriculum overhaul would be prohibitively expensive, the school board should adopt the voucher system.
questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that academic failure in public schools is caused primarily by inadequate curriculum

choices.label: B
choices.text: presents only two options without justifying the claim that no other options exist

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that what is true of the school board's budget is true of all individual schools

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider whether private schools would produce better academic outcomes than public schools

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes the expensiveness of one option for evidence that the other option is inexpensive

explanations.correct: The argument restricts the choice to two options — full overhaul or a voucher system — without showing these are the only possibilities. Targeted reforms, increased funding, teacher training programs, or hybrid models are all alternatives the argument ignores.
explanations.A: The argument mentions curriculum failure but does not explicitly attribute it to curriculum alone as a cause. More importantly, this is a peripheral premise issue rather than the central structural flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a false-dichotomy flaw: the argument manufactures an exclusive binary choice without justification.
explanations.C: No part of the argument moves from the school board's budget to individual school budgets; this composition/division flaw is not present.
explanations.D: Whether private schools perform better is relevant but its absence is a weakness in supporting the conclusion, not the structural flaw in the reasoning that restricts options.
explanations.E: The argument never implies the voucher system is inexpensive; this mis-describes what the argument does.

difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from unrepresentative sample with a plausible correlation-causation trap that students must rule out.
stimulus: A technology company surveyed 200 of its own software engineers and found that 85 percent preferred working remotely to working in the office. The company's CEO concluded that the majority of workers in the technology sector as a whole prefer remote work.
questionStem: The CEO's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes the employees' expressed preferences for evidence of what working arrangement produces the highest productivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about an entire sector based on a sample that may not be representative of that sector

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that remote work preferences remain stable over time

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that workers prefer office work as evidence that workers prefer remote work

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether the survey methodology adequately measured worker preferences

explanations.correct: The survey sampled only engineers at one company — a subset that may differ systematically from the broader technology sector, which includes workers in hardware, manufacturing, sales, and support roles. Generalizing from this narrow group to the whole sector commits the unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.A: The argument is about preferences, not productivity; this describes a scope shift that the argument does not make.
explanations.B: Correct. The sample is drawn from a single company's software engineers, which may not represent the diversity of roles and workers across the entire technology sector.
explanations.C: Temporal stability of preferences is a minor background assumption not central to the structural flaw in the generalization.
explanations.D: The argument does not argue from an absence of evidence; it draws a positive conclusion from positive survey data.
explanations.E: Survey methodology concerns are peripheral; the flaw is not in how preferences were measured but in the scope of the generalization from the measured group.

difficultyReason: Equivocation flaw on a key term used in two senses. Students must track the semantic shift rather than being drawn to a false-dichotomy or correlation trap.
stimulus: Historian: The law must be blind. Any system of justice that is not blind inevitably favors the powerful over the powerless. Our current legal system, however, is clearly not blind — judges regularly distinguish between categories of defendants based on their circumstances. Therefore, our legal system inevitably favors the powerful over the powerless.
questionStem: The historian's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents a conclusion about the entire legal system based on the behavior of some judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on an ambiguous term that is used in different senses in the premise and the conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without evidence that powerful defendants are treated more favorably than powerless defendants

choices.label: D
choices.text: mistakes a feature of legal systems in general for a feature of the current legal system in particular

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether a legal system that distinguishes among defendants could still treat them fairly

explanations.correct: 'Blind' in the premise 'the law must be blind' means impartial or unbiased — not favoring the powerful. But the argument then takes 'not blind' to mean 'makes distinctions among defendants,' which is a different sense. The equivocation on 'blind' drives the invalid inference.
explanations.A: The argument generalizes from judges' behavior to the system, but this is not the primary structural flaw — the equivocation on 'blind' is what makes the reasoning invalid.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Blind' shifts from meaning 'impartial' (normative sense) to 'makes no distinctions' (descriptive sense). The two senses are conflated, making the inference invalid.
explanations.C: The argument infers that the system favors the powerful; it doesn't assume this without evidence — it derives it via the flawed equivocation. This choice misdescribes the structure.
explanations.D: The argument does not move from general to particular; it moves from a general principle to a conclusion about the current system. The flaw is equivocation, not a scope shift of this kind.
explanations.E: This correctly identifies a gap in the argument but describes a missing consideration rather than the logical flaw — the equivocation — that makes the inference invalid.

difficultyReason: Circular reasoning flaw with a well-disguised trap that names an absent flaw (false dichotomy) and one that is plausible but describes a peripheral weakness.
stimulus: Nutritionist: Organic produce is healthier than conventionally grown produce because food grown without synthetic pesticides is better for human consumption. And food grown without synthetic pesticides is better for human consumption because organic produce — which avoids synthetic pesticides — is inherently healthier.
questionStem: The nutritionist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes without justification that synthetic pesticides are the only difference between organic and conventional produce

choices.label: B
choices.text: bases its conclusion on a study that may not represent all types of produce

choices.label: C
choices.text: supports its conclusion by simply restating the conclusion in different words

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a characteristic of some organic produce as a characteristic of all organic produce

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents only two options — organic or conventional — without considering intermediate alternatives

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'organic is healthier' to 'food without synthetic pesticides is better' and then back to 'organic is healthier because it avoids synthetic pesticides.' Both the premise and the conclusion express the same claim in rephrased terms; the argument is circular.
explanations.A: This concern about other differentiating factors would be relevant to a causal argument, but here the problem is circularity, not an omitted variable.
explanations.B: No study is cited in the argument; this choice fabricates a premise that isn't present.
explanations.C: Correct. The nutritionist's reasoning traces a loop: organic is healthier → avoiding pesticides is better → organic is healthier. This is textbook circular reasoning.
explanations.D: The argument makes no distinction between some and all organic produce; it speaks universally, so no composition error is committed.
explanations.E: The argument does not set up a dichotomous choice between organic and conventional — it simply asserts the superiority of organic. No false dichotomy is present.

difficultyReason: Scope shift / composition flaw with a tempting correlation-causation trap. Students must notice the argument moves from individual to group level.
stimulus: Each individual species in a coral reef ecosystem is highly adaptable to changing ocean temperatures. It follows that a coral reef ecosystem, considered as a whole, is highly adaptable to changing ocean temperatures.
questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes the fact that ocean temperatures are changing for evidence that coral reef ecosystems will not survive

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider whether the rate of temperature change affects the adaptability of individual species

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats what is true of each part of a whole as necessarily true of the whole itself

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about ocean ecosystems in general based on evidence drawn only from coral reefs

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without justification that adaptability to temperature change is the most important feature of an ecosystem

explanations.correct: Even if every individual species can adapt, the ecosystem as a whole might not be adaptable — species interact in complex webs; losing even one species can cascade and destabilize the whole system. The argument commits the composition fallacy: attributing a property of each part to the whole.
explanations.A: The argument never mentions whether reefs will survive; this introduces a conclusion the argument does not draw.
explanations.B: The rate of change is a peripheral consideration and its absence does not constitute the structural flaw in the reasoning.
explanations.C: Correct. This precisely names the composition fallacy: inferring a property of the whole from properties of its individual parts.
explanations.D: The argument does not generalize to all ocean ecosystems; it reasons only about the coral reef. No overgeneralization across ecosystems is committed.
explanations.E: Adaptability's relative importance is irrelevant to the logical move from parts to whole that constitutes the flaw.

difficultyReason: Appeal to inappropriate authority / ignores counter-evidence flaw with a trap that correctly names ad hominem but misapplies it, and one that describes the conclusion rather than the reasoning error.
stimulus: Art critic: The painting currently attributed to Vermeer cannot be authentic. Professor Holt, the world's foremost expert on seventeenth-century Dutch painting, has declared it a forgery. No one is more qualified than Holt to make such a determination, so the painting is definitively a forgery.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the credibility of those who believe the painting is authentic rather than addressing their reasons

choices.label: B
choices.text: concludes that the painting is a forgery without examining the painting itself

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats an expert's opinion as conclusive proof while failing to consider that even qualified experts can be mistaken

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses the question of who is most qualified to assess a painting with the question of whether that assessment is correct

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about this painting based on characteristics of seventeenth-century Dutch paintings in general

explanations.correct: Being the most qualified expert does not make one's judgment infallible. The argument treats Holt's opinion as definitively settling the matter, ignoring the possibility that even the most qualified expert can err, especially in contested authentication cases.
explanations.A: The argument does not attack anyone who disagrees with Holt; it simply accepts his opinion. No ad hominem move is made.
explanations.B: The argument does not specify whether the critic examined the painting; this introduces a factual claim not supported or denied by the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument moves from 'most qualified' to 'definitively correct,' which is unwarranted — expertise reduces error but does not eliminate it.
explanations.D: This is a tempting paraphrase of the flaw, but it misframes the error as a confusion about questions rather than identifying the unwarranted inference from expertise to certainty. (C) is more precisely correct.
explanations.E: The argument makes no claim about seventeenth-century Dutch paintings in general; it focuses exclusively on this painting's attribution.

difficultyReason: Absence-of-evidence flaw with a plausible scope-shift trap. Students must recognize the argument treats a lack of findings as positive evidence of absence.
stimulus: Archaeologist: No written records from the Harappan civilization have been successfully deciphered. This strongly suggests that the Harappan people did not use writing as a tool for administrative governance — if they had used writing for governance, we would certainly have found decipherable records of it by now.
questionStem: The archaeologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about ancient administrative practices based on evidence drawn only from the Harappan civilization

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that the absence of deciphered records proves the absence of written governance, without ruling out that such records exist but remain undeciphered

choices.label: C
choices.text: mistakes a feature of some ancient civilizations for a feature of all ancient civilizations

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to provide an alternative explanation for how the Harappans administered their civilization

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that written governance is necessary for a civilization to achieve a high level of administrative complexity

explanations.correct: The archaeologist infers from 'no deciphered records' to 'no written governance.' But absence of decipherment is not absence of records — Harappan script remains undeciphered, meaning governance records could exist but simply not yet be understood. The argument treats failure to decode as evidence of nonexistence.
explanations.A: The argument draws no comparison to other civilizations; it makes no generalization beyond the Harappan case. No overgeneralization is present.
explanations.B: Correct. The flaw is treating the inability to decipher existing records as equivalent to the nonexistence of such records — a version of the absence-of-evidence fallacy.
explanations.C: The argument makes no claim about other civilizations; this flaw is not committed.
explanations.D: The archaeologist need not provide an alternative governance model; failing to do so is not a logical flaw in the negative conclusion being drawn.
explanations.E: The argument does not claim written governance is necessary for administrative complexity; it only claims the Harappans probably didn't use writing for governance. This flaw is not present in the stimulus.
